author: Philip K. Dick
card_summary: In a Hanoi where the Party has won the global war, Tung Chien is a mid-level functionary at the Ministry of Cultural Artifacts. A legless war-veteran peddler compels him by law to buy a herbal remedy, and sells him what is described as something to rest eyes wearied by official monologues.
page_summary:
In a Hanoi where the Party has won the global war, Tung Chien is a mid-level functionary at the Ministry of Cultural Artifacts. A legless war-veteran peddler compels him by law to buy a herbal remedy, and sells him what is described as something to rest eyes wearied by official monologues. Chien is meanwhile handed a career test: two student essays, one orthodox and one heretical, and he must say which is which. Watching the Absolute Benefactor's nightly televised address that evening, he takes the powder — and the Leader's image is replaced by a mechanical construct with pseudopodia and a squawk-box. He reports himself to the Security Police, who analyse the substance and tell him it is not a hallucinogen at all but a phenothiazine, an anti-hallucinogen. Tanya Lee then arrives and explains: the water supply carries a hallucinogen, Datrox-3, continuously and everywhere; the phenothiazine merely lifts it. Her group has twelve members who have each seen something different — the Clanker, the Gulper, the Bird, the Climbing Tube, the Crusher — twelve realities and one hallucination, which is the wrong way round and which no theory they have accounts for. She tells him which exam paper is orthodox, having bugged his superior's office, and reveals that the whole test was a loyalty probe. Her price is that when he is invited to the Leader's stag dinner he should go medicated and look. He goes, and sees. What crosses the room is neither a man nor a machine: something he can only make out sidelong, that drains and loathes and steps on people as it passes. It addresses him inside his head, tells him it founded the Party and the anti-Party alike, that it has picked everyone out and needs only to watch. He recognises it as the hunter of the Arabic quatrain in the exam paper — death, and God, one thing. He goes to the veranda and tries to jump; it stops him with what becomes a human hand, tells him not to do its work for it, and promises to deprive him of everything he possesses before killing him. Sent home drunk in disgrace, he tells Tanya only that they cannot win. They go to bed. Undressing, he finds the marks on his shoulder where it held him, and they are bleeding.

**Why it matters.** The story's theological move is to collapse a distinction rather than draw one. The thing at the villa claims to have founded the Party and the anti-Party, those for and those against, and to need only to watch because the arrangement is automatic. Chien's recognition is that the hunter of the quatrain, death, and God are one force, and that both poems he was made to grade were describing it. What keeps this from being merely bleak is the ending's cruelty of detail: it stops his suicide not out of mercy but because he would be doing its work early, and it promises to take everything from him first. The marks that bleed are the story's only supernatural evidence, and they arrive after all the arguing is over.

*The last exchange is domestic and tender — she asks for a towel, he asks if she can continue — and it is played straight. He has perhaps hours. The story ends with him hugging her to him.*

structure.form: novelette in five movements, from bureaucratic comedy to theophany
movements: Hanoi street and Ministry: the compulsory purchase, and the two exam papers.
The apartment: the snuff, the Clanker on the screen, the police, and the lab result that inverts everything.
Tanya Lee's explanation: Datrox-3 in the water, twelve realities, and the terms of her bargain.
The Yangtze River villa: the stag dinner, and the thing that crosses the room.
The veranda and after: the refused suicide, the promise, and the marks that bleed.
structure.point_of_view: third person tight on Chien, who is a careerist and knows it. The comic register of the opening is doing structural work — the further the story travels, the less the tone protects him.
structure.central_inversion: The drug is not the hallucinogen; the water is. What Chien takes does not distort his perception, it restores it. Everything he has ever seen on television, including the Leader, was the induced state.

characters.name: Tung Chien
characters.note: An opportunist without illusions about his own opportunism. His curiosity is what undoes him, and he identifies it as a career-terminal condition before indulging it.

characters.name: Tanya Lee
characters.role: clerk at the Ministry; member of the group
characters.note: Not anti-Party, as she insists. Her group wants only to know who or what is leading them. She supplies the drug, the answer to the loyalty test, and the moral pressure.

characters.name: The Absolute Benefactor of the People
characters.note: Given three incompatible identities in one story: a hundred-and-twenty-year-old Asian on television, a Caucasian ex-New Zealand Communist named Fletcher with a wife, and the thing at the villa. The story does not reconcile them.

characters.name: The legless peddler
characters.note: Uses the veterans' privilege statute to compel the sale — the drug reaches Chien through a law the regime itself made.

characters.name: Darius Pethel
characters.note: Actually Higher Secpol Inspector Judd Craine, according to Tanya Lee, who names him as chief assistant at a war-crimes trial in Zurich.

characters.name: Kimo Okubara
characters.note: Contemptuous throughout, and the one who ejects Chien at the end as a common drunk.

settings.name: Hanoi
settings.note: Capital of a world the Party won; San Francisco was a battle, the Pentagon remnants are in the Catskills, and the last reaction is in the red hills of Oklahoma.

settings.name: Chien's conapt
settings.note: Where the television cannot be switched off and a building warden calls when attention lapses.

settings.name: The Yangtze River villa
settings.note: Site of the stag dinner. Deliberately bawdy and faintly ridiculous — the theophany happens at a party with nude waitresses and too many toasts.

motifs: Two poems as the story's own commentary: an Arabic quatrain on death as a hunter who chooses one of many hours, and Dryden's line about music untuning the sky. Both are supplied as exam material and both turn out to describe what Chien later meets
Compulsory attention: the television that cannot be turned off, the warden who calls when you look away
Twelve realities and one hallucination — the group's central puzzle, stated and never solved
The stigma: marks left on the shoulder where it held him back, which bleed at the end
Career advancement as the mechanism of damnation — he is promoted for passing the test that destroys him

The thing at the villa claims to have founded the Party and the anti-Party, those for and those against, and to need only to watch because the arrangement is automatic. Chien's recognition is that the hunter of the quatrain, death, and God are one force, and that both poems he was made to grade were describing it. distinctive_terms.label: Taoist
distinctive_terms.note: The cover story for the San Fernando school: courses that appear to teach Taoist philosophy.

pkd_on_this_work.summary: Dick returned to this story repeatedly in the Exegesis as evidence about his own experience, and believed it had drawn official attention to him.

evidence.quote: My 3-74 experiences are an outgrowth of my Palmer Eldritch experience of over ten years earlier. "Faith of Our Fathers" shows this too; I knew Him to be real … but o…
evidence.reading: The strongest claim in the file: Dick reads the story as showing that he already knew the deity to be real, years before 2-3-74. A Lane B statement about a Lane A text, and it must not be collapsed into a claim about what the story means.

evidence.quote: Except in such works as Ubik, "Faith of Our Fathers," 3 Stigmata, TMITHC, "Electric Ant," Tears,
evidence.reading: Dick's own canon of the works in which, on his account, the absolute event shows through. A list worth taking seriously as his periodisation of his own output.

evidence.quote: Something of this seems hinted at in "Faith of Our Fathers," too: lies, delusions (induced by drugs), tyran…
evidence.reading: A more cautious formulation from elsewhere in the Exegesis — 'seems hinted at' rather than 'I knew Him to be real'. The two registers should be kept side by side.

evidence.quote: I believe it was my novels and stories (such as "Faith of Our Fathers" and THE THREE STIGMATA) which alerted the aut…
evidence.reading: Dick attributing official surveillance of himself to this story and Palmer Eldritch. Sutin corroborates that these were the two works Dick most often suspected in this regard.

evidence.quote: Reprint rights on "Faith of Our Fathers" runs about $150 to $200
evidence.reading: Declining an unpaid comic-book adaptation. Included because the file's other material is so heavily metaphysical that the ordinary business of authorship is worth keeping visible.

pkd_on_this_work.caution: The Exegesis passages were written after 2-3-74 and read the story through it. The 1967 story was composed for an anthology on a commission; nothing in the letters of that period claims a revelation.

criticism.summary: Thin in this archive, which is itself notable for a story of this standing.

evidence.author: Christopher Palmer
evidence.quote: Tolley also discusses "Faith of Our Fathers" (1967, CS5), a story involving a very ambiguous de…
evidence.reading: Palmer relaying Michael Tolley (1980) on the story's ambiguous deity. The Tolley original is not in the archive — a gap, since he appears to be the substantive critical treatment.

evidence.author: Lawrence Sutin
evidence.quote: Phil most often suspected, in this regard, were The Penultimate Truth (1964) … and "Faith of Our Fathers," a story written for Harlan Ellison's SF antholo…
evidence.reading: Corroborates Dick's belief that this story attracted official attention, and confirms the Dangerous Visions commission.

contradictions.summary: Dick states both that the story shows he knew the deity to be real, and that the theme is only 'hinted at' in it.

claim_a.text: "Faith of Our Fathers" shows this too; I knew Him to be real

claim_b.text: Something of this seems hinted at in "Faith of Our Fathers," too

contradictions.note: Both are Exegesis entries. The Exegesis is not a single position but a decade of argument with itself, and flattening it into one verdict would misrepresent the document.

contradictions.summary: The story gives the Leader three mutually exclusive identities and never reconciles them.

claim_a.text: a hundred-and-twenty-year-old Asian leader on television

claim_b.text: Thomas Fletcher, a Caucasian from the New Zealand Communist Party, with a wife

contradictions.note: A third identity — the thing at the villa — is given as well. Tso-pin explains the televised image is refined for ideological purposes, which accounts for the first two and not the third.

open_questions: Michael Tolley's 1980 discussion is cited by Palmer as the substantive treatment and is not in the archive. Worth acquiring.

Dick believed this story and The Three Stigmata drew official attention to him. Is there anything in the letters of 1967-1968 contemporaneous with that belief, as against the later retrospective claims?
The story was commissioned for Dangerous Visions. Ellison's introductions to that anthology are substantial and are not in the corpus; they would be contemporary reception by a fellow writer.

reading_provenance.note: Close reading of the primary text plus attributed evidence from the archive. Candidate: not yet promoted to canonical.
